name: Ráday Street
address: Ráday utca, 1092 Budapest (Kálvin tér to Boráros tér)
intro: Ráday utca is a street in Ferencváros that runs from Kálvin tér towards Boráros tér and is just over a kilometre long. It is known mainly for its restaurants, but it also holds a Reformed theological library, a handsome Secession courtyard house and the Ráday Street Theatres Meeting (RUSZT), a festival of independent theatre first held in November 2022.
about: Ráday utca lies in District IX, Ferencváros, and links Kálvin tér with Boráros tér. Hungarian Wikipedia gives its length as 1.01 km, lists the postcodes 1092 and 1093 and calls it known mainly for its restaurants. A 2022 article by We Love Budapest describes a constantly bustling street of restaurants and bars that also offers plenty of cultural activity.

The best-known courtyard is the Schmalz-udvar at number 26, on the corner of Köztelek utca, a rental block with Secession features. We Love Budapest describes its courtyard with stained-glass windows, gallery walkways, a flower-patterned stone floor and wrought-iron railings. On the corner outside, a plaque by the painter and graphic artist László Dinyés commemorates Lajos Kossuth.

Number 28 is an institutional address. It is the home of the Ráday Library and the Bishop’s Office of the Reformed Church’s Danube District (Dunamelléki Egyházkerület), and the theology faculty of Károli Gáspár Reformed University and the Ráday Collection are listed there too, according to Hungarian Wikipedia.

Theatre has its own place on the street. The Ráday Utcai Színházak Találkozója, usually shortened to RUSZT, is a festival that brings the independent theatre scene to Ráday utca; its first edition ran from 4 to 6 November 2022. The festival has been held again since, but dates and programme can change between editions, so check the organisers’ channels rather than relying on an old listing.
tips: For festival visits, check the organisers’ own channels for the current RUSZT programme; dates and programme can change between editions.

Look above the shopfronts. The Hild and Ybl houses and the Schmalz-udvar at number 26 are residential buildings, so enjoy them from the pavement and respect the residents if a gateway happens to be open.
The Ráday Library and the theology faculty at number 28 belong to the Reformed church and university. Contact them directly if you want to know whether a visit is possible.
The street starts at the Kálvin tér end, which makes it an easy evening extension to a day around the Inner City and the Great Market Hall.
Terraces and traffic arrangements on a busy restaurant street change over time, so treat any photo or map as a snapshot rather than a guarantee of what you will find.

history.intro: The street has had several names and builders. Hungarian Wikipedia, drawing on Budapest street-name lexicons, records its names from the late eighteenth century onwards.

sections.heading: From country road to Ráday utca
paragraphs: The earliest names are all place names: Haraszti út in 1777 (Harasztierstrasse in German), Ócsai út in 1782, Kecskeméti út in 1784 and then Soroksári utca from 1804, a name still recorded in 1874. The present one dates from 1906 and honours the collector and poet Gedeon Ráday (1713–1792).

sections.heading: Houses of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries
paragraphs: Most of the buildings the sources single out date from between the 1840s and the 1910s. Hungarian Wikipedia lists a residential building at numbers 11–13 designed by József Hild in 1847 and remodelled by Ferenc Wieser in 1861, and another at number 18 from 1875 by Miklós Ybl. Two buildings of 1911 are named as well: number 9 by Gyula Fodor and number 14 by Dezső Dénes and Artúr Mellinger. The Szent Imre College at numbers 43–45 was built in 1910 to plans by Imre Szőts and Albin Siegel.

We Love Budapest dates the Schmalz-udvar to around 1910 and says it was commissioned by the landowner and entrepreneur Károly Schmalz, after whom the courtyard is named. The article names the architect as János Bach, who died in 1925.

sections.heading: A memorial plaque and a young festival
paragraphs: The Kossuth plaque by László Dinyés has marked the Schmalz-udvar corner since 2002, installed by the District IX municipality for the 200th anniversary of Lajos Kossuth’s birth. We Love Budapest adds that a commemoration is held there every 15 March.

RUSZT is a recent addition. We Love Budapest reports that its first edition in November 2022 grew out of the 2019 Startfeszt and involved five theatres using six venues: Itt és Most Társulat, Kettőspont, MáSzínház, Pinceszínház and Stúdió K Színház.

name: Rákóczi Square Market Hall
intro: The Rákóczi téri Vásárcsarnok is a neighbourhood food market in Józsefváros, built in 1894 and opened to shoppers in 1897 as the second of the large market halls in District VIII. A fire destroyed the building in 1988, and after rebuilding it reopened in 1991. It is still a working market for local shoppers.
about: The Rákóczi téri Vásárcsarnok, or Rákóczi Square Market Hall, stands at Rákóczi tér 7-9 in Józsefváros, District VIII. It is one of the municipal market halls on Piaconline, the website of the market operator, and it lent its name to the Csarnok negyed, the Hall Quarter, a Józsefváros neighbourhood created in 2012.

Piaconline’s listing counts 47 units, among them restaurants, general food shops, greengrocers, butchers and delicatessen, bakers, dairy, pickles, fish and game, a pharmacy and drugstore, and fashion goods. The operator’s page names tram and the M4 metro among the ways to reach the hall; a current route planner gives details.

The operator’s history describes how the hall was first arranged: a main entrance on Rákóczi tér wide enough for a horse-drawn carriage to unload, 375 permanent and 55 temporary stalls, a storage cellar, corner pavilions for officials, a first-aid post and restaurants, and rented flats above. Opening days, including holiday closures, are published on the hall’s Piaconline page, which is the place to check before you go.
tips: Check the Piaconline page for the Rákóczi téri Vásárcsarnok for the current opening days and holiday closures before you set out.
It is a working neighbourhood market, so go to buy lunch or ingredients rather than to sightsee; the listing includes several food stalls and restaurant units.
Combine it with the Great Market Hall for a comparison between a large central hall and a local one.
The operator’s page names tram and the M4 metro among the ways to reach the hall; use a current route planner for details.
Be considerate when photographing: stallholders and shoppers are going about their day.

history.intro: The hall belongs to the generation of municipal market halls built in Budapest in the 1890s, and its story includes a long decline, a fire and a rebuilding.

sections.heading: A site proposed in 1890
paragraphs: The professor Győző Czigler of the Technical University suggested the site in 1890. István Rozinay and Pál Klunzinger designed the hall, which was built in 1894 and opened to shoppers in 1897, the second of the large halls to go up in District VIII, according to the operator’s history.

sections.heading: Decline and fire
paragraphs: Trade had dwindled so far by 1936 that closing the hall or converting it into a swimming pool was planned, though neither idea was carried out. In the night of 6 May 1988 a fire broke out and the building burned down.

sections.heading: Rebuilt and renamed
paragraphs: The ruin was not demolished. The architects György Tokár and György Hidasi drew up the plans for its renovation, and the hall reopened on 25 July 1991. In 2012 the market gave its name to the Csarnok negyed, the Hall Quarter.

name: Ecseri Flea Market
intro: The Ecseri piac, which a 2020 We Love Budapest article calls the largest of Budapest’s flea markets, lies on Nagykőrösi út at the south-eastern edge of the city. Furniture, tools, cameras, Soviet-era relics and antiques fill its open-air and indoor stalls. The used-goods market dates its official founding to 1897 and has stood on this site since the 1960s.
about: The Ecseri Használtcikk Piac, officially the Nagykőrösi úti Használtcikk Piac, is a used-goods and antiques market at Nagykőrösi út 156 in District XIX. The operator’s history places it on the border of Pesterzsébet and Kispest, far from the central tourist districts, and Piaconline lists it among the market sites it runs.

A 2020 visitor article from We Love Budapest describes a mix of open-air and indoor stalls, often packed to the brim, selling furniture, tools, toys, trinkets, antiques, Soviet-era relics, old cameras and unusual jewellery. Piaconline’s listing of the site separates its units into storage units, antiques dealers and restaurants. The operator’s history says the market has a reputation as the place where almost anything turns up, and names a knight’s armour among the finds.

Getting there takes some planning. The operator’s page lists buses 54, 55, 84E, 89E, 294E, 607 and 608. The 2020 article describes a journey of about 30 minutes from the city centre, with buses 54 and 55 from Boráros tér and 84E and 89E from Határ út, and an overpass from the bus stop leading to the entrance. It also recommends Saturday morning, says weekday pickings are thinner, notes that vendors took only cash at the time and says prices are negotiable.
Check the Piaconline page for the market’s current opening days and holiday closures before you go.
tips: Check the Piaconline page for the Nagykőrösi úti Használtcikk Piac for current opening days and holiday closures before travelling.
A 2020 visitor article recommends Saturday morning and says vendors only took cash then; bring cash, check whether that has changed, and expect to bargain politely.
The operator’s page lists buses 54, 55, 84E, 89E, 294E, 607 and 608; check a current route planner, as services change.
Wear sturdy shoes and allow plenty of time; stalls are spread across open-air and indoor areas, and bargains are found by wandering.
Ask before photographing a stall or its owner.

history.intro: The operator’s history traces the market through three sites and several changes of stock since the late nineteenth century.

sections.heading: Three sites since 1897
paragraphs: The used-goods market of the capital dates its official founding to 1897. It began on Teleki tér in outer Józsefváros and stayed there until 1950, when it was moved to Ecseri út in outer Ferencváros, next to the former Mária-Valéria estate. In 1964 the building of the József Attila housing estate pushed it out again, to Nagykőrösi út on the Pesterzsébet–Kispest border, where it still stands. The history says ideology played a part in the moves alongside town planning.

sections.heading: From second-hand clothes to antiques
paragraphs: Clothes and shoes were what buyers mainly sought in the market’s first fifty to sixty years. From the 1960s imported Western European clothing, mostly smuggled in, and technical goods took a larger share. By the 1980s the biggest business was done by art dealers, who bought old ornaments and apparently worthless pictures from itinerant traders. The market was turning from an ócskapiac, a junk market, into a bolhapiac, a flea market of the kind found in large Western European cities.

name: Szilágyi Dezső tér Reformed Church
intro: The Reformed church on Szilágyi Dezső tér is a neo-Gothic red-brick church on the Buda bank of the Danube in Víziváros. Designed by Samu Pecz and consecrated in 1896, it has a slender 62-metre tower and a roof of glazed Zsolnay tiles. Hungarian Wikipedia calls it the second-largest Reformed church in Budapest.
about: The Szilágyi Dezső téri református templom is the church of the Budapest-Buda Reformed congregation and stands freely in a park on Szilágyi Dezső tér in Víziváros. It is a protected monument, and Hungarian Wikipedia describes it as the second-largest Reformed church in Budapest after the one on Kálvin tér.

Seen from outside, it is a red-brick, centrally planned neo-Gothic church with a 62-metre tower beside the front facade, a ten-sided drum with a pointed tent roof over the central space, buttresses and pointed-arch windows. The heritage register adds that the main doorway is a pointed arch with a gable and an ornate wrought-iron grille, and that a pointed-arch bridge links the tower to the church at gallery level. The congregation says the plan is pentagon-like and that the church seats about 600; Samu Pecz also designed its fittings and furniture.

Brown, yellow and green glazed tiles from the Zsolnay factory cover the roof, and together with the tower they make the church a landmark of the Buda riverside. In front stands a neo-Gothic memorial fountain to Pecz, with the pedestal and fountain by Béla Rerrich and the statue by Lajos Berán, according to the heritage register.

The church is a working place of worship rather than a museum. The congregation’s website lists regular services and an audioguide, and it is the best place to ask how and when the interior can be visited.
tips: Treat the church as a place of worship: keep your voice low, dress modestly and avoid photographing during services.
Check the congregation’s website (gyulekezet.hu) for service arrangements and for how to visit the interior; it also links to an audioguide.
Walk around the church to see the tower, the drum and the glazed roof tiles, and look for the Pecz memorial fountain in front.
Samu Pecz also designed the Great Market Hall and, with Frigyes Schulek, worked on the Matthias Church; both have pages on this site and make a good architectural pairing.
St Anne’s Church on Batthyány tér is a further Víziváros church to add to a walk along the Buda embankment.

history.intro: The church was built for a young congregation. The congregation’s own history, a heritage register entry and Hungarian Wikipedia between them give a clear outline, though they differ slightly on the construction years.

sections.heading: A congregation and a square
paragraphs: Reformed worship in Buda is older than the church, but the Budapest-Buda Reformed congregation was only taking shape in 1885, and its first communion service was held on 5 April that year. The city handed over Fazekas tér, today Szilágyi Dezső tér, for a church on 19 June. Four designs were submitted and Samu Pecz’s was chosen, with some modifications. The building was financed by a national fundraising campaign, and the congregation’s account says Emperor Franz Joseph gave 100,000 gold crowns.

sections.heading: Building and consecration, 1893 to 1896
paragraphs: The square had to be filled in first, and construction began on 13 June 1893. The congregation says building was finished in 1895 and that the church was consecrated on Palm Sunday 1896. The heritage register gives 1893–1896 as the construction years, and Hungarian Wikipedia gives 1893–1896 in its summary box but 1893–1895 in its text, so the end date depends on whether completion or consecration is counted.
The three larger bells were ordered from the Bochum steel works. The congregation says the heaviest, at 1,890 kg, is the largest Reformed bell in Budapest.

sections.heading: Wartime damage, restoration and a poet’s wedding
paragraphs: The church was hit several times during the siege of Buda in 1944–45. According to the congregation it had served as a munitions store and so became a military target, and the tower was left damaged and in danger of collapse. Services were possible again by Palm Sunday 1946. Restoration of the roof tiles was done by 1979 and the whole programme was complete by 1986, followed by exterior renovation between 2001 and 2014 and interior work between 2019 and 2021.
The church also figures in Hungarian literary history: the poet Endre Ady married Berta Boncza here on 27 March 1915, with the minister Benő Haypál officiating.

name: Hungarian Electrotechnical Museum
intro: The Electrotechnical Museum occupies a former transformer station at Kazinczy utca 21 in the Jewish Quarter. A branch of the Hungarian Museum of Science, Technology and Transport, it follows the history of electrification and lighting in eight permanent exhibitions, with working old devices and a courtyard of vintage neon signs. Check the official page for its current status.
about: The Elektrotechnikai Múzeum, which the Hungarian Museum of Science, Technology and Transport (MMKM) also calls the Elektrotechnikai Gyűjtemény, is housed in a former transformer station. The transport museum’s English page calls it the Museum of Electrical Engineering and says the building is a national monument with an art deco stone floor and Zsolnay tiles. Industrial Heritage Hungary mentions an art deco staircase with green Zsolnay tiles on the walls leading up to the exhibition rooms.

Eight permanent exhibitions in four rooms follow the development of electrical engineering, with a focus on Hungarian industry: railway electrification, lighting technology and transformer production. Industrial Heritage Hungary lists early transformers, generators, motors, electric meters, rectifiers, condensers, fuses and relays, as well as electric signal fences, measuring and alarm equipment and barbed-wire fences from the Iron Curtain. A separate room is given to early household appliances and lighting.

Part of the display is hands-on. The museum describes an influence machine and hand-cranked dynamos that visitors can try, and some of the devices are over a century old and still work. The Jedlik room is the most interactive part, and the museum organises physics demonstrations for schools and the public. Posters honour Hungarian pioneers: Ányos Jedlik, Miksa Déri, Ottó Titusz Bláthy and Károly Zipernowsky, known for the transformer, and Kálmán Kandó, the railway electrification pioneer.

In the courtyard the Neonparade shows old neon advertisements treated as works of art, among them the Patyolat swan, the Csemege basket and a winking owl from a second-hand bookshop. Kazinczy utca lies in the Jewish Quarter, near the synagogue, and the museum’s English page places it about 200 metres from Rákóczi út and the Uránia cinema. The museum’s own pages give differing information about visiting arrangements, so confirm them with the museum before planning a visit.
tips: Check the official MMKM page for the Elektrotechnikai Gyűjtemény for current visiting arrangements before you go; the museum’s own pages give differing information, so confirm them with the museum.
Industrial Heritage Hungary says the museum regularly runs physics demonstrations for schools and the public; ask the museum whether any are planned during your visit.
The museum is on Kazinczy utca near the Kazinczy Street Orthodox Synagogue, so it combines well with a walk through the Jewish Quarter.
Look into the courtyard for the Neonparade exhibition of old shop signs, a good subject for photographs; ask staff about photography rules inside.
The Dohány Street Synagogue and Szimpla Kert, which have their own pages, are two other well-known stops in the Jewish Quarter.

history.intro: The building began as part of the infrastructure that brought electricity to Pest. Sources agree on its original function but differ on some dates, so the account below states which source says what.

sections.heading: A transformer station of 1934
paragraphs: Industrial Heritage Hungary describes the museum as occupying a 30/10 kV transformer station commissioned in 1934 and used until the end of the 1960s. It names the architects Ágost Gerstenberg and Károly Arvé and describes the design as Bauhaus-style. The museum is in the right wing, which once housed the 10 kV transformers, relays and switches, while the 30 kV system was in the left wing.

We Love Budapest describes the U-shaped building as having supplied direct current to central Pest for about half a century. That does not match the 1934 to late-1960s dates above, so the length of the station’s working life should be treated as approximate.

sections.heading: The electricity company at Kazinczy utca 21
paragraphs: The Budapest Stock Exchange Museum says the former headquarters of the Budapest General Electricity company, founded in 1892, was at Kazinczy utca 21. The company’s converter stations turned alternating current into direct current, and during the First World War they supplied several streets, Kazinczy utca among them.

The same page adds that the city opened its own power plant at Kelenföld in 1914, that the company was redeemed by the city in 1918 and that it went into liquidation on 1 January 1921. It says the former headquarters is now a museum of electrical engineering. The sources do not explain how the company’s seat relates to the 1934 station, so the two accounts are given here side by side.
